title: Progress in quantum telescopes
authors: David R. Gozzard, Fiona H. Panther, Andrew G. White
abstract: Classically, the angular resolution of a telescope is limited by its diffraction limit: the ratio of its observing wavelength to its diameter. Developments in quantum information theory over the past decade have uncovered quantum-optimal measurement methods that enable super-resolution imaging beyond the diffraction limit, and many laboratory-scale demonstrations of these methods have been performed over the past decade, culminating in the recent first on-sky demonstration of quantum-enhanced astronomical imaging. In this Review, we detail the current progress and achievements of these theoretical and experimental results, discuss the astronomical science cases motivating the development of higher resolution telescopes, summarise the technological challenges facing the practical application of quantum imaging technologies to astronomy, and present a vision for the realization of \emph{quantum telescopes} with imaging resolutions orders of magnitude better than current observatories.
summary: This review surveys the progress toward building 'quantum telescopes' capable of super-resolution imaging beyond classical diffraction limits. It leverages quantum information theory to show that quantum measurements can extract phase information inaccessible to classical methods. The paper outlines the theoretical advances, technological hurdles, and future vision for revolutionizing astronomical observation.
main_problem: The primary challenge is overcoming the classical diffraction limit in telescope angular resolution, which is fundamentally constrained by the ratio of wavelength to aperture diameter.
main_result: Quantum information theory suggests that quantum-optimal measurement methods can enable super-resolution imaging, potentially achieving resolutions orders of magnitude better than current observatories.
method: The review details the application of quantum estimation theory, specifically utilizing the Quantum Cramér-Rao Bound (QCRB), to derive fundamental limits on achievable angular resolution.
model_or_system: The system under study is astronomical imaging using large telescopes across optical and infrared wavelengths. The theoretical framework compares classical direct imaging (DI) with quantum-enhanced measurement protocols.
key_observables: Angular resolution, Point Spread Function (PSF), and the achievable precision quantified by the Fisher Information (FI) and QCRB.
important_parameters: Wavelength ($\lambda$), aperture diameter ($D$), and the target resolution approaching one microarcsecond ($1 \mu	ext{as}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the quantum state of the light field is the only accessible resource, and that quantum measurement techniques can be practically implemented in astronomical settings.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the classical Rayleigh criterion for resolution. Figure 2 compares the Fisher information for source separation using classical vs. quantum Cramér-Rao bounds, showing the quantum advantage.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the classical diffraction limit. It then introduces quantum metrology to derive super-resolution bounds, discusses the theoretical tools (QFI, QCRB), reviews laboratory demonstrations, and concludes with a vision for practical quantum telescopes.
why_interesting: This work bridges quantum information theory (quantum estimation, QCRB) with large-scale physical systems (astronomy/optics), providing a roadmap for quantum enhancement in observational science.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Illustration of the Rayleigh criterion for resolution of an imaging system. The blue traces depict the intensity profile of the Airy disks resulting from two point sources through the PSF of a telescope. The red dashed trace depicts the summed intensity profile of the two Airy disks. Left-to-right: objects are resolved, objects are at the Rayleigh limit, and objects are unresolved. The Abbe and Sparrow limits are described in Section 1.1.1.

Figure 2. Fisher information for the separation of two weak thermal sources according to the classical and quantum Cramér-Rao bounds based on (2019a). The separation is given in multiples of the beam waist of the imaging system optics.
Figure 3. Generalised schematic of an intensity interferometer based on the Hanbury Brown-Twiss (HBT) effect.

Figure 4. Generalised schematic of a Stankus-Nomerotski-Slosar-Vintskevich two-photon amplitude interferometer. Two-photon states from two optical sources are interfered at the beam splitter in each observing station. Correlations between the measurements at the two stations determine the source visibility. Measurement data can be transmitted between the stations electronically.
Figure 5. Generalised schematic of a SPADE imaging system. Each mode is separated and coupled to a separate photon-counting detector.
